newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami, conservatives haggle over cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami, conservatives haggle over cabinet.

text.p: Iran's new president Mohammad Khatami is haggling behind closed doors with conservatives on a compromise cabinet which could pass parliamentary approval with little opposition, diplomats said on Thursday.
"Compromise is the order of the day," a Western diplomat said. "There is a lot of manoeuvring behind the scenes."
Iran's fifth president, who took the oath of office on Monday, has by law until August 18 to submit his cabinet list to the Majlis or national assembly for approval.
Khatami has been working on the list since his landslide election in May. The 270-member conservative-dominated house next meets on Sunday.

"The last thing the president wants now is to present a cabinet which would be voted down by parliament," one diplomat said. "It makes political sense to present a list which has been discussed with the Majlis."

Earlier in the week conservative deputies hinted at their displeasure with Khatami's failure to consult them before drawing up his list, which analysts and diplomats said could be modified over the Moslem weekend which started on Thursday.
Former Majlis speaker Mehdi Karrubi said: "I'm sure that Mr Khatami will have no problems with the Majlis for approving his cabinet members."
He said that he and "all of Mr Khatami's friends" had been in contact with deputies for "the rapid approval of the cabinet," Iran News daily reported.
Khatami's predecessor Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who is also seen as a moderate among Iran's ruling Shi'ite Moslem clergy, had members of his cabinet rejected by parliament.
Khatami himself was forced to resign in 1992 as culture minister for failing to halt what was seen as a Western cultural invasion of the Islamic republic.
Analysts said some of the names were floated in the press in recent days to test responses.
One said: "A debate was started and the influences of each view is currently being weighed by the pesident."
Khatami, 54, won Iran's top elective post with an overwhelming majority over conservative Majlis speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri.

Hardline conservatives are opposed to some of Khatami's possible candidates including United Nations ambassador Kamal Kharrazi who on Monday told Reuters he had been approached to become Foreign Minister.

Deputy Seyed Hashemi criticised Khatami's apparent desire to give Energy Minister Bijan Namdar Zangeneh a new ministry. Zanganeh has been tipped to run the oil affairs of the world's third largest oil exporter, replacing Gholamreza Aghazadah.

But the apparent nomination of Ataollah Mohajerani for the Culture and Islamic Guidance Ministry, a sensitive post if Khatami intends to make good on promises of social reforms, seemed to be causing the most trouble, diplomats said.
Mohajerani came under severe attack in the late 1980s for proposing direct talks with Iran's declared enemy the United States.
Without giving names, Karrubi said: "My assessment is that all the nominees will receive the necessary votes, but the number of favourable votes cast will depend on the proposed minister."
